Meanderings & Digressions · Data stories · November 2026

Same Miles, Different Shape

Two build-ups to the Dallas Half Marathon, as told by my watch

On July 9, 2025, I went out in 87-degree rain and ran pyramid intervals because an app told me to. It was week one of an eight-week plan. I covered 4.2 miles at 9:18 a mile and felt every one of them.Everything here comes from my Strava log: {{n}} runs and {{total:.0f}} miles between that first run and {{updated}}. Paces are moving pace.

Five months later I ran the Dallas Half Marathon in 1:38:08. Now I’m training for it again, five weeks out, with a broken leg somewhere in between. I wanted to know how this year’s build compares with last year’s, so I lined the two up.

Seventeen months, one dot per run

Each dot is a run, placed by date and distance. Hover over a dot for the details. The open circle is the race I haven’t run yet.The first build is easy to read. The dots climb from July to December, the long runs peel away from the weekday runs in September, and the whole thing ends at 13.1.

The second is messier. A mile time trial in January, a month of nothing in March while a leg healed, then a long flat stretch of five-mile runs through a Texas summer. The long runs only start to lift off in late September.

The balance is the same

A training block works a little like a savings account. You make deposits, and on race day you find out what the balance buys. So I added up the deposits, starting 22 weeks before each race.

Oddly though, despite the broken leg, the two accounts hold almost exactly the same amount. Five weeks out last year I had run {{m25:.0f}} miles in {{r25}} runs. Five weeks out this year: {{m26:.0f}} miles in {{r26}} runs. The gap is {{diff:.1f}} miles, which is less than a warm-up.

The deposits are not

Last year I started from nothing and ramped hard. Weekly mileage tripled between July and November, and by five weeks out I had already gone past 12 miles {{tw25}} times, the last of them a full 13.

This year I started with a base and coasted on it. In the first thirteen weeks I banked {{ed:.0f}} more miles than last year ({{e26:.0f}} against {{e25:.0f}}). In the five weeks since, I’ve given {{ld:.0f}} of them back ({{l26:.0f}} against {{l25:.0f}}). The long run is the clearest difference: {{lg26:.0f}} miles is my longest so far, where last year it was {{lg25:.0f}}.

Here’s the uncomfortable part. A half marathon doesn’t care much about the balance. It cares about the big deposits, and this year I haven’t made one over {{lg26:.0f}} miles.

What the heat costs

There is one thing in this year’s favor. My average pace is {{pd}} seconds a mile quicker than at the same point last year, in weather that was, if anything, slightly hotter: {{t26:.0f}} degrees on average against {{t25:.0f}}. In Dallas the thermometer does a lot of the pacing.

Across both years, every extra 10 degrees has cost me about {{slope:.0f}} seconds a mile. The fitted line puts a 50-degree run at {{f50}} and a 95-degree run at {{f95}}.This overstates the heat a little. My cool runs also come late in a build, when I’m fitter, so temperature is getting credit for some of the training. I haven’t tried to separate the two.

That makes me hypothesize that this year’s engine is at least as good as last year’s. The fastest efforts point the same way at the short end and the opposite way at the long end.

Last year’s 5K and 10K bests were both set inside the race itself. This year’s 5K came on an ordinary Tuesday morning run, the most recent one in the data.

What the race looked like

It is worth remembering what all those long runs bought. The first mile was the slowest at 8:34. Then I settled, and ran the back half much faster than the front: miles one through six averaged {{first6}}, miles eight through thirteen averaged {{last6}}. That is {{halfgap}} seconds a mile quicker, with my heart rate pinned in the mid-160s for the last hour.

How much of that was me, and how much was the course?

Some of it was the course. After a short drop out of downtown, the route climbs {{up:.0f}} feet over {{upmi:.1f}} miles to its high point just past mile {{himi:.0f}}, and I ran that stretch at {{uppace}}. It then gives all of it back over the next {{downmi:.1f}} miles, which I ran at {{downpace}}. The fast back half was partly gravity.

The last mile and a half is the tell. The road turns up again for {{lastft:.0f}} feet to the finish, and I held {{lastpace}}, well inside what I had averaged on the first climb.

You can only finish like that if the distance itself is no longer a question. Last year, by race day, I had covered 13 miles or more three times in training.

Five weeks

In the last five weeks of the 2025 build I ran another {{rest25:.0f}} miles, race included, with long runs of 13, 13 and {{restlong:.0f}}, and finished the block at {{full25:.0f}}. That is the part of the gray line the orange one hasn’t drawn yet.

The balance is fine. The next few Saturdays decide what it buys.
